defaults.ws.2: Letting every client run cases their own way
defaults.ws.3: Disclaimer: The interfaces presented in this case study are representative mockups and may not exactly reflect the production application. Certain elements have been modified or recreated to comply with confidentiality and NDA obligations.
defaults.ws.4: I led product and design on Kriyam Workspace, a feature on Kriyam's field investigation platform that lets clients reshape the app around how they already work, instead of learning to work the way the app expects. Kriyam runs three different kinds of investigations — Pre & Post, Claims and Financial Services. All three come down to the same basic act: send someone out to verify something on the ground. Almost nothing else about them lines up. Workspace exists to close that gap.
defaults.ws.5: Problem: Every Client Was Speaking Their Own Language
defaults.ws.6: It usually showed up in the first ten minutes of a demo. Someone on the client's side would land on a column labelled "Case ID" and pause — not confused, exactly, just unconvinced. Their team had been calling it something else for years, long before Kriyam existed. And Case ID was the easy one. The same thing happened with the second person tied to a case, with the individual checks that made up a bigger investigation, with half the vocabulary on the screen.
defaults.ws.7: That's the part that's easy to miss unless you've sat through it yourself — this was never really a complaint about labels. Pre & Post, Claims, and Financial Services aren't the same workflow in different outfits. They run under different logic, answer to different people, and care about entirely different fields. But for a long time, Kriyam pushed all three through one fixed case list — same columns, same section names, same structure, no matter who you were or which format you were running. Every client had to learn Kriyam's language before they could get on with speaking their own.
defaults.ws.8: You could see the cost in small, recurring moments rather than one dramatic failure. A new hire taking a little longer than they should to feel at home in the tool. Support fielding the same "can you just rename this for us" request every few weeks. A client spending their first month on the platform translating our screen into their own paperwork instead of just using it. None of it looked like a crisis. All of it added up.
defaults.ws.10: We didn't need a formal study to see this one — it was in every client conversation we had, all the time. And it wasn't limited to what showed up on screen, either. This was baked into how teams already talked to each other on the ground, on calls, in their own internal paperwork, long before Kriyam ever entered the picture.
defaults.ws.11: The case number was the easiest one to spot. Customer ID to one client, Case ID to another, Investigation ID to a third — the same field wearing three different names depending on whose office you walked into.
defaults.ws.12: The second name on a case wasn't safe either. Co-applicant to one client, Joint applicant to another — same person, different word, depending entirely on whose paperwork you were reading.
defaults.ws.13: Even the smallest unit of work had multiple names floating around. Subcase to one, verification to another, a point to a third — three words for the exact same piece of work.
defaults.ws.14: None of these clients were wrong. Each had simply settled on their own vocabulary years before we showed up, and every time they used Kriyam, we were quietly asking them to unlearn it.
defaults.ws.15: Solution: A Workspace of Your Own
defaults.ws.16: So instead of asking clients to adopt Kriyam's language, we let them keep their own. Workspace gives every client a version of Kriyam that's genuinely theirs from the first day — the naming, the layout, the structure — something they shape themselves instead of something they request through a support ticket.
defaults.ws.17: It starts the moment a new account is created, before anyone on the team has even logged in. The admin sets things up section by section: name one, add the case fields that belong to it, then move to the next — until the whole structure matches how this client actually organises a case, and setup is done.
defaults.ws.18: None of it has to be right on the first pass. A preview button shows the case list exactly as the team will see it — the same sections, the same fields, laid out for real rather than described in a form. This is also where visibility and order get settled before anyone else logs in: hide a field nobody needs, move a column up if it matters more than the rest.
defaults.ws.19: A client rarely stops at one workspace. One account can run several at once — a Claims workspace next to a separate Financial Services one, however the business actually splits its work — and all of them get created and managed from the same settings screen. Moving between workspaces was never meant to feel like switching accounts: the side navigation lets a team jump from one to another inside a single session, no logout and no fresh login required, with users and vendor agencies carrying over automatically so nobody's set up twice.
defaults.ws.20: And it doesn't stop once a case goes live. Open an actual case, and the same sections an admin built during setup are right there on the case details page — labelled the way this client already talks, arranged the way this client decided. Because no client gets everything right on day one, none of it is locked in: order and visibility can still be changed from the case details page itself, long after the workspace first launched.
defaults.ws.21: Worth saying plainly — Workspace doesn't touch what stage a case moves through next. That's a different feature, Workflow, and it deserves its own write-up rather than a passing mention here.
defaults.ws.23: A client running Pre & Post and Claims side by side usually isn't running two separate businesses — more often, it's the same field executives and the same vendor agencies doing the work, just under two different rulesets. So while every workspace keeps its own database and its own case data, users and agencies can be pulled in from a client's other workspaces rather than set up from zero each time. The one thing that doesn't cross over is the configuration itself — forms and case structures stay fully separate, on purpose, because that's exactly what each workspace exists to control.
defaults.ws.24: Nothing about this was meant to be permanent.
defaults.ws.25: The easy way to build an admin setting is to treat it as something configured once, carefully, and left alone. We didn't want that here. Client processes shift, teams reorganise, and someone always ends up wanting to rename a column six months after go-live. So every decision made at first setup — every label, every hidden section — stays just as editable a year in as it was on day one.
defaults.ws.26: Impact: Less Time Teaching the App
defaults.ws.27:

onboard a new team

defaults.ws.29:
Less time to a client's

defaults.ws.30: The clearest signal so far is time. Onboarding a new team onto Kriyam now takes roughly 30% less time than it did before Workspace existed. When the app already speaks a client's own language from day one, there's simply less to explain, and less for a new hire to quietly translate in their head before they can get to work.
defaults.ws.31: Two more numbers back that up. Support tickets asking us to rename a field or add a column are down 85-90% since Workspace launched — probably the most direct read we have on whether the translation tax actually went away. And the time from account creation to a client's first live case has dropped by around 60%, so clients are getting up and running without needing us in the loop nearly as much as they used to.
defaults.ws.32: Adoption tells its own story, too. From the very first clients onto Workspace, people started spinning up multiple workspaces on their own, unprompted — exactly the signal we wanted, that this was solving something real rather than sitting there as an option nobody touches.
defaults.ws.33: It's still early, and we don't have years of data behind this the way an older product might. But every workspace a client sets up on their own terms is one less thing our team configures by hand on their behalf, and one less reason someone's first week on Kriyam feels like learning a foreign system instead of just doing their job.
defaults.bu.3: Buy it. Use it. Sell it. — A trust-first resale marketplace designed to remove fraud, friction, and fear from second-hand commerce in India.
defaults.bu.5: Resale in India has a trust crisis.
defaults.bu.6: Platforms like OLX, Quikr, and Facebook Marketplace have unlocked a massive market for second-hand goods in India. But they've also created a breeding ground for fraud. Fake listings. Stolen photos. Payment scams. Robbery during physical meetups.
defaults.bu.7: The process hasn't changed in years. A seller lists something. A buyer wants it. They either ship it blindly and hope for the best — or they physically meet up in a parking lot and hope nobody gets robbed. Neither option inspires confidence.
defaults.bu.8: What should be simple — "I have something I don't need, you want it" — becomes complicated, risky, and often abandoned altogether.
defaults.bu.9: of marketplace revenue is lost to seller fraud and fraudulent listings on peer-to-peer platforms globally
defaults.bu.11: crimes traced to a single OLX fraud network in India over just 18 months, exposing how organised the scams have become
defaults.bu.13: daily active users on OLX India — a scale that makes fraud prevention not optional, but existential
defaults.bu.15: Common fraud patterns on existing platforms
defaults.bu.17: Fraudsters steal product images from real listings, post them at attractive prices, collect a "reservation deposit," and vanish. Buyers lose money before they've even seen the product.
defaults.bu.19: Scammers use fake courier receipts to pressure buyers into paying delivery fees upfront. No product ever ships. The courier company doesn't exist.
defaults.bu.21: OLX's own workaround — meet in person — created its own danger. Buyers carrying cash to inspect high-value items like phones or bikes became targets for robbery and assault.
defaults.bu.23: Fraudulent buyers send forged payment screenshots to sellers, pressure them to ship first, then disappear. Sellers hand over the product and never see the money.
defaults.bu.25: Build the trust layer that resale was missing
defaults.bu.26: The ask was clear: design a resale marketplace where neither buyers nor sellers have to trust a stranger — because the platform does the trusting for them. No physical meetups. No payment anxiety. No fake listings.
defaults.bu.27: The constraints were tight. Four weeks. One person handling both design and project management. No time for long iteration cycles — but no shortcuts on the thinking.
defaults.bu.29: Every step mapped. Every edge case considered.
defaults.bu.30: We started where all good design starts — with people. Not assumptions about people. Actual people. Two distinct types of personas, two entirely different relationships with resale.
defaults.bu.32: Sellers here aren't mass merchants. They're someone whose baby has outgrown a toy, someone upgrading their phone, someone clearing out a room. They're listing one product, maybe two. The flow needed to feel as simple as sending a WhatsApp message. Buyers, on the other hand, want assurance — they're looking for a deal, but not a gamble. Both personas shaped every design decision that followed.
defaults.bu.34: We mapped every journey — seller onboarding, product listing, buyer search, purchase, internal verification, logistics handoff, post-delivery inspection, returns, refunds, edge cases. What happens if a seller cancels after verification? What if a buyer raises a dispute at hour 47? We designed for the exceptions before we designed for the happy path.
defaults.bu.36: No low-fidelity digital wireframes. The time constraint was real, and the flow clarity was already there. We hand-sketched the critical screens, mapped the interactions, and moved fast into high-fidelity. Pragmatic — not lazy. The thinking happened on paper. The execution happened in Figma.
defaults.bu.38: Before touching product screens, we established the visual language. Colour palette, typography, logo — enough to make the product feel coherent and trustworthy without spending weeks on brand strategy. For a resale marketplace, visual trust signals matter. The brand needed to communicate reliability, not just aesthetics.
defaults.bu.40: Straight from brand foundation to high-fidelity screens. 70+ screens covering every user journey, every state, every edge case. Built to be handed off, not just presented.
defaults.bu.41: DigiLocker integration wasn't just a feature decision — it was the single move that solved the biggest design problem in the product: how do you trust a stranger on the internet?
defaults.bu.42: DigiLocker holds verified government documents for Indian citizens. By requiring seller verification through DigiLocker, we established real identity and real accountability — without building complex verification logic from scratch.
defaults.bu.44: The trust layer, designed screen by screen.
defaults.bu.45: Every screen had one job: remove a reason to distrust. For sellers, that meant a listing flow that felt guided, not overwhelming. For buyers, it meant surfacing the safety mechanisms — verification badge, escrow status, inspection window — at every decision point.
defaults.bu.46: From seller onboarding to post-delivery resolution — every flow, every state, every edge case. Built to be shipped, not just demonstrated.
defaults.bu.48: Identity verification via government-issued documents. No fake sellers. No fake products. Real accountability from the first screen.
defaults.bu.50: Guided listing for non-technical sellers. Photos, condition, price range. Simple enough for someone listing their first and only product.
defaults.bu.52: Browse, filter, and find verified products. Every seller carries the BUSEit verification badge — proof someone from our team has seen it.
defaults.bu.54: Buyer pays. Money holds in escrow. Nobody gets paid until the buyer confirms the product is what was promised. Trust built into the transaction itself.
defaults.bu.56: Our team visits the seller, verifies the product against the listing. Condition check. Authenticity check. Only then does it move to the buyer.
defaults.bu.58: Buyer gets 48 hours to inspect the product. If it doesn't match the listing — return it. Money goes back. Seller keeps accountability.
defaults.bu.60: Structured return process. We collect, we refund, we close the loop. No he-said-she-said. No ghosting. Just a clear resolution path.
defaults.bu.62: Full visibility from pickup to delivery. Buyers always know where their product is. Sellers know when their money is coming.
defaults.bu.64: Seller cancellations, failed verifications, payment disputes, late inspections. Every scenario designed — because real users don't always follow the happy path.
defaults.bu.66: What shipped. What's next. And why.
defaults.bu.67: A good MVP isn't about building less. It's about building the right thing first. Version 1 focused entirely on getting the trust mechanics right. Everything else was designed, thought through, and deliberately deferred.
defaults.bu.70: AI Image Verification — Reverse image search on every uploaded product photo to detect stolen images, recycled listings, and counterfeit products.
defaults.bu.71: Multi-Platform Listing Sync — Sellers list once on BUSEit and push to other resale platforms simultaneously with a single toggle. Same caption, same photos, zero extra effort.
defaults.bu.72: AI Predictive Pricing — Sellers set a price range and a time-to-sell deadline. The system reads market trends, suggests optimal pricing, and dynamically adjusts offers.
defaults.bu.73: Community & Bidding — Buyer and seller profiles, social discovery, and a bidding system for high-demand products where the highest bid in a set window wins.
defaults.bu.77: With four weeks and one person handling design and project management, low-fidelity wireframes would have been a third iteration of the same thinking. The user flows were mapped. The sketches were done. The value wasn't in more lo-fi artifacts — it was in getting to high-fidelity fast enough to catch real visual and interaction problems. Speed was the constraint. Clarity was already there.
defaults.bu.79: Building a custom identity verification system would have taken time we didn't have and trust we hadn't yet earned. DigiLocker is a government-backed platform that Indian citizens already use and trust. By integrating it, we borrowed credibility from an established system rather than asking users to trust a new one. One integration solved the biggest trust bottleneck in the product.
defaults.bu.80: Why make the escrow so explicit in the UI?
defaults.bu.81: Most platforms bury their payment protection in terms and conditions nobody reads. We made the escrow status a visible, persistent UI element throughout the buyer's journey — because if users don't know their money is protected, the protection doesn't build trust. Visible safety mechanisms change behavior. They give buyers the confidence to complete a purchase they'd otherwise abandon.
defaults.bu.82: Why design V2 features in the MVP phase?
defaults.bu.83: Features like AI image verification and predictive pricing weren't designed to ship in V1 — they were designed to stress-test the product architecture. If you only design for what you're shipping today, you paint yourself into corners that make V2 expensive to build. Thinking through the bidding system and multi-platform sync in advance meant the V1 information architecture could accommodate them without a full redesign later.
defaults.bu.86: BUSEit is currently in QC testing — not yet live with real users. The learnings here come from the design and internal testing phase. The most valuable insights didn't come from user data. They came from the moments where the design broke under its own logic.
defaults.bu.88: We could have added more seller options, more filter types, more customisation at every step. We didn't. The strongest decision we made repeatedly was choosing what to leave out. A listing flow with fewer fields isn't less capable — it's more usable for someone who's never sold anything online before.
defaults.bu.90: During design review, it became clear that building our own verification system would have introduced new trust problems while trying to solve existing ones. Leaning on an established, government-backed system meant users didn't have to trust BUSEit's verification process — they trusted something they already knew.
defaults.bu.91: Edge cases are the real product.
defaults.bu.92: The 70+ screens didn't all feel essential at first. But mapping scenarios like "seller cancels after physical verification" or "buyer raises dispute at hour 47" revealed friction points that would have been catastrophic in the live product. The happy path is 20% of the design work. The other 80% is everything that can go wrong.
defaults.bu.94: In traditional resale, there's ambiguity around when a buyer actually commits. Making the inspection window explicit — visible, time-stamped, clearly communicated — changes the psychological contract between buyer and seller. The buyer gets to inspect before the seller gets paid. That's a fundamentally different transaction, not a feature.
defaults.bu.96: See a little more? click the first button. Wanna know really really more, click the second one.

defaults.about.label: About
defaults.about.p1: The longer version involves a political science degree I don’t regret, a design certification I actually use, and five years of getting progressively more opinionated about hierarchy.
defaults.cap.label: Capabilities
defaults.cap.lead: Six things I’m reliably good at.
defaults.cap.1.title: UX Strategy & Research
defaults.cap.1.body: I run user interviews, contextual field studies and usability testing, then turn the findings into journey maps, personas and a prioritised problem statement — so the roadmap is built on evidence rather than assumptions.
defaults.cap.2.title: Product & Interaction Design
defaults.cap.2.body: I design end-to-end product flows, information architecture and interaction models for web, tablet and mobile — covering the edge cases, empty states and error paths, not just the happy path.
defaults.cap.3.title: Design Systems
defaults.cap.3.body: I build and document scalable design systems in Figma — tokens, components, variants and usage guidelines — so engineering ships consistent, accessible UI faster and the visual language holds as the product grows.
defaults.cap.4.title: Visual & Interface Design
defaults.cap.4.body: I set typography, colour, spacing and layout systems that give an interface a clear hierarchy and a distinct brand voice, with every visual decision doing measurable work for comprehension.
defaults.cap.5.title: AI & Emerging Technology
defaults.cap.5.body: I design for AI-assisted and agentic products — prompt and result patterns, confidence and citation cues, review and override controls — so users understand what the system did and stay in control of the outcome.
defaults.cap.6.title: Collaboration & Delivery
defaults.cap.6.body: I work alongside product managers, engineers and QA from discovery to release: annotated specs, design reviews, developer handoff in Figma and post-launch iteration based on analytics and user feedback.

kriyam.name: Kriyam.ai
kriyam.statRest: Faster Verifications with zero data leaks…
kriyam.lede: End-to-end field investigation — dispatch, track, collect, verify.

facts.v: Senior User Interface & User Experience Designer
Insurance & NBFCs, Operations & Compliance and Verfication Agencies

impact.p: Unstructured phone calls and WhatsApp dispatches were replaced with structured digital workflows—making case assignments instant and eliminating delays across every step.
Standardised forms and guided inputs removed reliance on manual data entry—significantly improving accuracy and reducing time spent on corrections.
All customer data is processed within a secure, encrypted environment—eliminating untracked sharing through intermediaries and ensuring full regulatory compliance.
Every action is automatically logged, giving teams complete transparency and audit readiness—without manual record-keeping.

overview: Insurance FCUs, TPAs, and investigation agencies operate in a high-stakes environment where every manual error, every undetected fraud, and every data leak carries direct financial and regulatory consequences. With crores lost annually to insurance fraud in India, IRDAI mandates around data protection tightening, and FCU teams stretched thin, the need for a structured, compliant verification process was not optional — it was critical.

Before Kriyam.ai, field verification was entirely ad-hoc. Cases were dispatched over phone calls, WhatsApp, and emails — with no traceability, no SLA control, and no audit trail. Customer personally identifiable information was being shared with agencies through unencrypted channels, creating serious regulatory exposure. Document forgery — tampered IDs, deepfake photos, fabricated certificates — went undetected because manual reviewers lacked the tools to catch what automated systems can flag in seconds. The result was a process riddled with inefficiency, liability, and compliance gaps.

To address this, I led the design of Kriyam.ai — a comprehensive web and mobile field verification platform built to replace these unsecured, untraceable workflows. The platform introduced location-traced case assignments, end-to-end encrypted data handling, and full auditability, bringing the entire verification process into compliance with India's DPDP Laws. By eliminating informal channels entirely, every verification became structured, accountable, and legally defensible.

The impact was immediate and measurable. Turnaround time dropped by 30%, reported errors fell by 80%, and data leakages reached zero. AI-powered case summarisation now saves clients 12 hours of work weekly, and overall productivity for field verification teams has tripled. Kriyam.ai transformed what was once an uncontrolled liability into a reliable, efficient, and fully compliant operation — giving agencies real control over their data and their risk.
role: As the Senior UI/UX Designer, I partnered closely with the product manager, a dev lead, a UI Designer, three developers, and a QA engineer to shape Kriyam.ai from concept through launch. My process was deeply collaborative and iterative, not linear.

The product manager identified the features we needed to build. From there, I took ownership of research and discovery — understanding the user context, mapping workflows, and designing the simplest, fastest, most user-friendly path to solve each problem.

Rather than handing off finished designs, I maintained continuous dialogue with the development team throughout their build process, reviewing their work, offering insights, and iterating together as implementation revealed new considerations.

Once features moved to QA, issues and edge cases came back to me for refinement. I worked closely with the QA team to understand what was breaking or confusing, and we'd refine both the design and implementation to fix it.

This constant feedback loop — product defining features, me designing and researching, developers building with my input, QA validating and flagging issues — became the rhythm that shaped how Kriyam.ai came together.

proteger.name: Proteger Collect
proteger.statRest: faster data capture with zero friction on the factory floor.
proteger.lede: End-to-end operational intelligence for manufacturers. Designed with factory workers, built for speed.

facts.v:
Web Application, Tablet &
Mobile Application (iOS & Android)
Factory Owners, Floor Workers, Maintenance Teams, QC, Operations Leadership

impact.p: Voice and vision based inputs eliminate manual entry friction. Factory workers capture data in seconds, not minutes, even in challenging conditions.

impact.h: 15 minutes saved per shift per worker
impact.p: Hands-free operation means workers spend less time on paperwork, more time on production. That's genuine productivity gain across your entire floor.
Predictive maintenance alerts mean issues are caught before machines fail. Maintenance teams respond faster. Factory keeps running.
Digital capture with AI validation removes human transcription mistakes. No more illegible notes or misplaced data.

overview: When we first stepped onto the factory floor, the reality hit hard. These weren't office workers with ideal conditions. Factory workers were battling poor lighting, wearing heavy gloves, safety helmets, and protective gear that made interaction with standard devices genuinely difficult. They were drowning in paperwork — maintenance logs written by hand, quality checks scribbled on clipboards, material tracking spread across scattered notebooks. This wasn't inefficiency born from laziness. It was a system fundamentally misaligned with how people actually worked.

We spent weeks on the floor, talking to workers one-on-one, watching them struggle. A maintenance technician trying to fill a form with thick gloves on. A quality inspector squinting in dim lighting to read small text. A line supervisor manually cross-referencing batch numbers across three different sheets. The pain points weren't subtle — they were baked into every interaction.

That's when the vision for Proteger crystallised. Not a generic factory app, but a suite purpose-built for real factory conditions. We started with Protegal Collect, our voice and vision-first data capture layer. But designing for gloved hands and poor visibility meant rethinking everything. Button sizes had to expand. Check sheets needed restructuring for large gloved fingers. Typography had to account for harsh overhead lighting and helmet-shadowed vision.

But the tablet was always meant to be a bridge, not the destination. The real target was voice. Hands completely free. No device to fumble with, no gloves fighting touchscreens. Just speak, and the system understands. We're building that future now — integrating advanced voice recognition and AI that learns factory-specific terminology, machine names, process jargon. Workers can stand at a machine, dictate maintenance notes, and data flows directly into the system.

Alongside Collect, we built Trace for material and batch tracking, giving full traceability through the production line. Then came the maintenance module — intelligent work management that predicts when machines need attention before they break. Quality management built on real-time digital records, not paper audits. And Analytics pulling everything together into live dashboards that give managers sight across the entire operation.
role: As UI and UX Designer on Proteger, my responsibility spanned the entire user experience across the suite — from initial research through design refinement and ongoing feature development. Our team conducted extensive user research directly on factory floors, visiting production facilities and conducting one-on-one interviews with maintenance technicians, quality inspectors, line supervisors, and equipment operators. I synthesised those insights into design principles that shaped every interface decision.

I owned the design of Proteger Collect, our voice and vision-first data capture layer, ensuring every button size, interaction pattern, and voice flow accounted for real factory conditions — poor lighting, gloved hands, safety gear constraints. I worked closely with the development team to translate those constraints into thoughtful solutions: accessibility-first interface design and the foundational voice architecture we're now building toward.

Across the full Proteger suite, I ensured cohesion — that Trace, the maintenance module, quality management, and Analytics all felt like one unified system rather than disconnected tools. My focus throughout was keeping the factory worker at the centre of every decision, designing not around their limitations but in respect of their reality.

The work wasn't unconstrained creativity. I navigated genuine boundaries throughout the project. Time constraints meant prioritising features that had the highest impact on factory operations. Enterprise compliance and regulatory requirements shaped how data flowed through the system and where it could be stored — everything needed to remain secure within internal infrastructure with zero external data leakage. Design language consistency had to bridge multiple modules while maintaining accessibility standards. These weren't obstacles to work around. They were conditions that made the design more rigorous, more honest, and ultimately more useful to the people using it every day.

goodbook.name: Goodbook
goodbook.lede: A comprehensive HR and attendance platform built for office-based workforces. Intelligence at the point of interaction.

facts.v: HR Departments, Finance Teams, Employees, Office Management.

impact.p: Facial recognition eliminates physical card dependency. Employees check in across office locations instantaneously, with liveness detection preventing spoofing.
Automated payroll generation and instant employee access to digital payslips removes the administrative overhead that previously consumed HR bandwidth.
AI-powered liveness detection and automated cross-referencing eliminate manual entry errors and buddy punching. The system is effectively tamper-proof.
End-to-end automation from check-in through payslip generation compresses what previously took days into hours. Finance and HR teams operate at genuine scale.

overview: The modern office HR function is drowning in process. HR teams manually reconcile attendance sheets. Finance teams spend days generating payslips from spreadsheets. Employees chase HR for paperwork. Check-in systems built around physical keycards create unnecessary friction — lost cards, slow queues, no actionable data. For small to mid-sized organisations with up to 250 employees, this overhead is particularly acute. Every hour spent on payroll administration is an hour away from strategic HR work.

Our research mapped the actual workflows. Employees wasted time fumbling with expired keycards or waiting in queues. HR spent disproportionate effort manually generating payslips — a repetitive, error-prone monthly ritual. Finance couldn't trust attendance data without manual verification. Office managers lacked visibility into who was present, creating scheduling complications. The system treated attendance as a compliance box to tick rather than business intelligence to act on.

Goodbook unified the entire employee lifecycle. We started with Gate Pass, our facial recognition check-in layer designed specifically for office environments. This wasn't novelty. We implemented liveness detection using AI and machine learning, requiring employees to perform specific randomised actions — smile, blink, turn to light. This prevents spoofing via image or video, ensuring attendance records remain trustworthy at scale. For office spaces with multiple entry points, this became the single source of truth for who is present and when.

The mobile application became the employee hub. Real-time attendance visibility. Leave management with granular categorisation — earned leave, casual leave, compensatory leave, maternity leave — with clear progress indicators showing remaining balance. Asset tracking showing company devices assigned to them. Expense submission for reimbursement. Critically, manual attendance adjustment when check-in failures occurred, eliminating the email-to-HR friction that previously consumed days of back-and-forth.

For HR teams, we built a comprehensive web platform. Complete administrative control over employee records, shift assignment, and policy management. Automated payslip generation connected to salary processing — the moment salary deposits, payslips are immediately available for employee download. Historical access to payslips across years and months. Company policies centralised and searchable. Real-time dashboards showing attendance patterns and compliance metrics.

Multi-location support meant that organisations with multiple office locations or flexible work arrangements had complete visibility. Geolocation tracking identified where employees were checking in from — office, home, or designated client location. For smaller teams managing hotdesking or hybrid arrangements, this provided the intelligence needed to optimise space and resources.

The design philosophy was straightforward: remove friction, not introduce it. Every feature traced back to a specific pain point. Every interaction was optimised for its context. The result was a system that gave HR teams back their time and gave employees clarity over their own employment data.
role: As UI/UX Designer, I led the complete product experience across three distinct platforms: the employee mobile application, the HR web platform, and Gate Pass facial recognition layer. Each platform served fundamentally different users in different contexts, demanding simultaneous attention to contrasting design requirements.

My process began with structured research across stakeholder groups — HR teams, finance, and employees across office locations. I mapped existing workflows, identified where administrative friction accumulated, and anchored every design decision in observable reality rather than assumption.

For the mobile experience, I designed with speed and clarity as the primary constraints. Employees needed immediate access to attendance status, leave balances, payslips, and expense submission without navigation overhead. For the HR web platform, the demands inverted — depth and control were necessary, with payroll automation, audit trails, and compliance dashboards designed for power users who needed to process data at scale.

Gate Pass required a distinct approach. Liveness detection needed to feel intuitive despite its sophistication — randomised action sequences delivered through clear on-screen instructions with real-time feedback, ensuring daily adoption without friction. I worked closely with the machine learning team to shape this interaction model end to end.

Throughout, data integrity and security shaped design decisions — access controls, audit visibility, and geolocation presentation were considered at interface level, not delegated to engineering. The full product was delivered within a compressed six-month timeline through disciplined prioritisation and rapid iteration with real users.
